Friday: At the church fete raffle stall, Joseph, fifteen, spent ten minutes choosing a ticket. Not the top one on the roll; he asked the aunty to tear out number 1407, his birthday. "Picked, not random. Better chance," he told Anjali.
Sunday: The winning number was announced: 2213. Joseph shrugged. "Close-ish. Wrong month."
Anjali read out the rules. "Every ticket had the same chance, Joseph. The draw doesn't know your birthday."
Next Friday: At the town fair, a stall sold scratch cards for a festival prize. Joseph stood there, hand hovering over the pile, looking for the lucky-looking one. Then he remembered Anjali's line, put his money back in his pocket, and bought a roasted corn cob instead.

qa.q: Which ticket number did Joseph ask for?
qa.a: Number 1407, his birthday.

qa.q: Why did picking his birthday feel like a 'better chance' to Joseph?
qa.a: Choosing it himself made the ticket feel special and connected to him, as if his choice could nudge a draw that was really pure chance.

qa.q: What was the turning point at the scratch-card stall?
qa.a: Remembering that the draw doesn't know his birthday, Joseph chose to keep his money and buy a corn cob instead.

qa.q: How might the aunty at the raffle stall see Joseph's careful choosing?
qa.a: The aunty might find it sweet or funny, knowing every ticket on the roll has exactly the same chance. 🙂

grounding: A teenage boy believes choosing his birthday ticket improves his raffle odds, then begins to question it.

passage:
Seema mole, you think you're lucky with numbers? Let me tell you about your Jomon Chachan at sixteen.
Every year at the church feast in our village there was a lucky draw, first prize a bicycle. Tickets were printed in order, but I made the seller let me choose. I would sit in the shade for an hour doing sums with my birth date, my house number, the day of the week. I was sure my number, chosen with so much effort, was stronger than a ticket someone just grabbed.
Three years running I chose. Three years running someone who grabbed won. Once it was my little cousin, who couldn't even read numbers yet.
I still remember her dancing next to that bicycle she couldn't ride. That day I finally understood: the drum doesn't care who thought hardest.

qa.q: What was the first prize at the church feast draw?
qa.a: First prize was a bicycle.

qa.q: Why did young Jomon believe his ticket was stronger?
qa.a: He had put an hour of sums and effort into choosing it, and that effort made his number feel as if it deserved to win more than a grabbed ticket.

qa.q: What was the turning point that changed Jomon's thinking?
qa.a: Seeing his little cousin, who couldn't even read numbers, win with a grabbed ticket showed him that effort had no hold on the draw.

qa.q: How might Seema use this story the next time a number feels lucky?
qa.a: Seema might laugh, then remember that the drum doesn't care who thought hardest, and be slower to trust a chosen number.

grounding: An uncle recalls believing, at sixteen, that a carefully chosen ticket beat random ones, until a small child's grabbed ticket won.

passage:
The school carnival was closing in twenty minutes, and Imran, fourteen, had exactly fifty rupees left: his bus fare home. At the scratch-card table a teacher was calling, "Last cards, win a football!"
Imran ran his fingers over the pile, lifting one, putting it back. "This one feels right," he said. "If I pick carefully, I'll get it."
His sister Parveen tugged his sleeve. "That's the bus money."
"I'm not guessing. I'm choosing."
"The card doesn't know you chose it," Parveen said. "The football is already printed on one card, somewhere in that pile."
Imran stared at the pile. Printed, fixed, before he even arrived. Slowly he put his hand back in his pocket, still gripping the fifty.

qa.q: How much money did Imran have left?
qa.a: Exactly fifty rupees, his bus fare home.

qa.q: Why did 'This one feels right' seem convincing to Imran?
qa.a: Touching and choosing the card made Imran feel his care could steer the result, as if effort could beat pure chance.

qa.q: What choice did Imran face at the table, and what helped him make it?
qa.a: He had to choose between the card and his bus fare; Parveen's point that the winning card was already printed helped him keep the money.

qa.q: What was it like for Parveen, watching Imran at the table?
qa.a: Parveen was probably worried about getting home, and could see clearly what Imran couldn't in that moment: the prize was already fixed on one card.

grounding: A teenage boy with only his bus fare believes carefully choosing a scratch card improves his odds, until his sister points out it is already fixed.

passage:
The festive sale at the Lucknow mall had a counter by the escalator: spend five hundred rupees, scratch a card, maybe win a scooter. Bhupen, fifteen, had spent his birthday money on shoes and earned one card.
The attendant held out the top card. "No, wait," Bhupen said. He riffled through the pile, pulled one from near the bottom, put it back and chose its neighbour. "This one feels right."
His cousin Alka rolled her eyes. "They're all printed already. The winners were decided in some factory."
"Yeah, but I picked it. That's different from being handed one." He scratched slowly with a coin, corner first, the way he had planned.
Better luck next time, the card said.
"I rushed the choice," he muttered, already eyeing the shoe shop's next five hundred.

qa.q: Where did Bhupen pull his first chosen card from?
qa.a: From near the bottom of the pile; then he put it back and chose its neighbour.

qa.q: How does Bhupen feel about choosing his own card, and why?
qa.a: Bhupen feels hopeful and in control when he picks the card himself, saying "This one feels right" as if his careful choice could change the result.

qa.q: At the moment Bhupen blames his "rushed" choice, what better choice could he make?
qa.a: He could remember Alka's point that every card was printed beforehand, accept that his picking changed nothing, and decide not to spend another five hundred chasing a card.

qa.q: How does Alka see Bhupen's careful card choosing?
qa.a: Alka finds it silly and a bit tiring to watch, because she knows the winners were fixed long before Bhupen touched the pile.

grounding: It shows a teenage boy believing that choosing his own scratch card, and scratching it carefully, improves his odds on a game of pure chance.

"Mummy, I'm not taking the ticket Gurleen brought. I'll go down and choose mine myself."
"Nilesh, it's the society Diwali tambola. Every ticket costs fifty, every ticket has fifteen numbers."
"But Gurleen just grabbed any. She didn't even look. I need 7 and 21 and lots of low numbers. Low numbers come early."
Gurleen laughed from the sofa. "Come early? The caller pulls them out of a bag, bhaiya."
"Last year I let Papa choose and I didn't even get a line. This year I'm picking."
"So if I swap tickets with you," Gurleen said, "does the bag start liking me instead?"
Nilesh paused. "That's different. I studied mine."
Mummy handed him the fifty. "Go. But tell me after how your studied ticket did."

qa.q: Which numbers did Nilesh want on his ticket?
qa.a: He wanted 7 and 21 and lots of low numbers.

qa.q: How does Nilesh feel about his own chosen ticket, and why?
qa.a: Nilesh feels confident about the ticket he studied and picked, and last year's disappointment with Papa's choice makes him determined to choose this time.

qa.q: What choice could Nilesh make at the moment Gurleen offers to swap tickets?
qa.a: He could take up her challenge honestly, swapping or comparing both tickets after the game, which would show that a chosen ticket does no better than a grabbed one.

qa.q: Why might Mummy let Nilesh go and choose instead of arguing?
qa.a: Mummy seems to want Nilesh to see the result for himself; asking him to report back lets the game teach him without a lecture.

grounding: It shows a teenage boy convinced that choosing and studying his own tambola ticket gives him better odds in a game decided by chance.

passage:
"I'm choosing my own raffle number this time. 27. My birthday."
"Kamal, the numbers are drawn from a pot," said Zubin, his cousin, as they stood at the mela stall. "The pot doesn't know your birthday."
"But if I pick it, it's more likely. Last year the uncle gave me a random one and I lost."
"Everyone lost except one person."
"Exactly. I didn't choose. This time I'm choosing."
"Two hundred tickets. One prize. Your number has the same chance as the uncle's number."
"It feels better, though."
"It feels better. It isn't better."
Kamal paid for ticket 27 anyway, holding it like it was warm. At nine they read out the winner: 143. Kamal stared at his ticket. "Maybe I should've picked 143."
Zubin laughed so hard he had to sit down.

qa.q: How many tickets were there?
qa.a: Two hundred.

qa.q: Why did Kamal feel choosing 27 made winning more likely?
qa.a: He felt more in control and hopeful picking his birthday number, so it seemed luckier than a random ticket.

qa.q: What does Zubin point out, and why does it matter?
qa.a: That every number has the same chance in the pot, so choosing a number feels better but doesn't change the odds.

qa.q: How does Zubin see Kamal's reaction to 143?
qa.a: Zubin finds it very funny that Kamal still thinks picking a number would have helped.

grounding: A teenage boy believes choosing his own raffle number improves his odds in a pure draw.

passage: At the Pongal fair last year there was a stall with scratch cards: pay ten rupees, scratch three boxes, win a toy or a phone. I was fifteen and sure I had figured it out. I didn't take the top card like everyone else. I asked for one from the middle of the pile, then one from the bottom, then one that felt warm. I thought choosing carefully gave me an edge. My cousin Keerthana watched me spend my whole hundred rupees of pocket money, one card at a time. I won a plastic whistle. She said, "Hemant, the cards don't know which one you picked." I argued all the way home. Later, in maths, we learned about chance, and I felt my face go hot remembering the warm card.

qa.q: What did Hemant win?
qa.a: A plastic whistle.

qa.q: Why did Hemant choose cards from the middle and bottom of the pile?
qa.a: Hemant felt clever and confident, believing careful choosing gave an edge in a game of pure chance.

qa.q: What would you tell Hemant before the next fair?
qa.a: That picking a particular card doesn't change the odds, so decide beforehand whether to play at all, knowing it is only chance.

qa.q: How did Keerthana see the scratch cards?
qa.a: Keerthana saw clearly that the cards don't know which one is picked, and watched, worried, as the pocket money went.

grounding: A teenager recalls believing that carefully choosing scratch cards improved the odds, and spending all the pocket money.

passage:
School counsellor's note, Class 11, 21 January
Ujjwal came to me this morning, worried about his friend Omkar. Omkar has been spending his lunch money on an online number game that promises big prizes. I spoke with Omkar at lunch. He was calm and confident: he said he always picks numbers from his own "system" of dates, so his odds are better than people who let the app choose. He has lost about two thousand rupees over three weeks but believes he is "close to cracking it." I showed him that each draw is random and that his chosen numbers have exactly the same chance as any others. He went quiet. With his agreement, I called his parents this afternoon, and we will all meet tomorrow. I have also reported the site to the principal.

qa.q: How much has Omkar lost over three weeks?
qa.a: About two thousand rupees.

qa.q: Why does Omkar feel confident about the number game?
qa.a: He feels calm and in control, believing numbers chosen from his own system of dates give better odds than letting the app choose.

qa.q: What steps did the counsellor take, and why do they matter?
qa.a: Showed Omkar that each draw is random, called his parents the same day with his agreement, and reported the site, so he doesn't face it alone.

qa.q: How was Ujjwal feeling when he came to the counsellor?
qa.a: Ujjwal was worried about his friend and cared enough to ask an adult for help.

grounding: A counsellor records a teenage boy who believes his own chosen numbers beat a random draw, and the same-day steps taken.

passage:
Saturday.
Diwali tambola at our society tonight. Tickets were given free to every family. Mummy picked up one for me from the pile, but I refused it. I had to choose my own. I spent ten minutes going through the stack looking for one with my birthday number, 17, and my lucky 7. I'm Raghav, the boy with the lucky numbers, everyone knows. Chinmay just grabbed the top one.
Chinmay won the first line.
I didn't win anything.
Later I told Papa it wasn't fair, I had chosen so carefully. He asked, "Does the caller know which ticket you picked?" Obviously not. "So does choosing change which numbers come out?" I didn't want to answer that. But it doesn't. Chinmay's random ticket had the same chance as mine.

qa.q: What did Chinmay win at the tambola?
qa.a: Chinmay won the first line.

qa.q: Why did Raghav spend ten minutes choosing his ticket?
qa.a: He felt hopeful and in control, believing that picking his birthday and lucky numbers would improve his chances.

qa.q: What did Papa's question help Raghav see, and how could he use it next time?
qa.a: That the caller doesn't know which ticket he chose, so choosing changes nothing; next time he can just take any ticket and enjoy the game.

qa.q: How might Chinmay see his win?
qa.a: Chinmay probably sees it as pure luck and fun, since he just grabbed the top ticket.

grounding: A teenager's diary shows him believing that choosing his own tambola ticket with lucky numbers gives him better odds.

passage: At the temple fair in Thrissur, the youth club was running a lucky draw: fifty coupons, one prize, a new bicycle. Jomon had saved his pocket money for weeks. "I'm choosing my own number," he told Harish, pushing through the crowd to the stall. The man held out a box of folded coupons. "Take any." Jomon shook his head. "Can I have number 14? It's my birthday." The man laughed and searched until he found it. Jomon held it tight, sure the bicycle was his. Harish took one without looking. "Why didn't you choose?" Jomon asked. "What's the difference?" Harish said. "One ticket gets pulled. Every ticket is one out of fifty." At eight o'clock the draw was announced. Number 31. Neither of them. passage:
The spring fair at the school in Uppsala had one real prize: a new bike in the raffle, twenty kronor a ticket.
Ulla bought hers from the top of the book, number 214, and wandered off to the waffle stand.
Abebe didn't. He leafed through the whole book, frowning, while the younger seller shifted from foot to foot. "Not 215. Not 216. Too close to hers." Finally he picked 777 from deep in the back.
"Does it matter?" Ulla asked, with syrup on her fingers.
"Of course. Anyone can take the next ticket. I chose this one." It felt obvious to him: effort had to count for something.
At four, the head teacher pulled a stub from the box.
"Two hundred and fourteen!"
Ulla shrieked. Abebe looked down at his carefully chosen 777 and felt strangely cheated, as if the box had ignored his work.

qa.q: What number did Ulla buy?
qa.a: Ulla bought number 214 from the top of the book.

qa.q: Why did Abebe feel cheated when 214 was drawn?
qa.a: Abebe had put effort into choosing 777, so it felt unfair that care and choice made no difference to a random draw.

qa.q: What could Abebe remind himself before buying a raffle ticket next time?
qa.a: Every ticket in the box has the same chance, so time spent choosing adds nothing; buy one for the fair and enjoy the day.

qa.q: How does Ulla see the choice of ticket?
qa.a: Ulla doesn't think it matters and takes the next ticket, then wins anyway, which shows the draw was pure chance.

grounding: Shows a teenager who believes choosing his own raffle number carefully gives him better odds.

passage:
The school mela had nine stalls, and Class 10B's was the spinning wheel: ten rupees a spin, land on the gold slice and win a big box of chocolates.
Chaitanya had already spent forty rupees. Mahima, running the stall, offered to spin for him to save queue time.
"No, no. It has to be me," he said. "I've worked out the speed. Medium push, starting from the red slice."
He pushed. The wheel clacked past gold and stopped on Try Again.
"Too fast," he muttered. "Next one slower."
"You know it's random, right?" Mahima said. "The kid before you spun it with his elbow and nearly won."
"That's luck. Mine's a method."
He pushed again, slowly. Clack, clack, clack. Try Again.
Chaitanya stood staring at the wheel, one hand still hovering, as if it owed him an answer.

qa.q: How much had Chaitanya already spent at the wheel?
qa.a: Chaitanya had already spent forty rupees.

qa.q: Why did Chaitanya insist on spinning the wheel himself?
qa.a: Chaitanya felt confident that a worked-out push could steer the wheel, so letting someone else spin felt like giving up control.

qa.q: What could Chaitanya try to test the method before spending more?
qa.a: Chaitanya could watch how often gold comes up for different spinners, including the elbow spin, and see there is no difference.

qa.q: How does Mahima see Chaitanya's method?
qa.a: Mahima sees the wheel as random and seems both amused and a little concerned, pointing to the elbow spin that nearly won.

grounding: Shows a teenager who believes his own spinning technique improves his odds on a chance wheel.

passage:
Dear Yamini Chechi,
You'll laugh, but I'm serious. When Ammavan went to buy his lottery ticket at the stall near the bus stand, he let me choose from the rack. The man said just take the top one. I didn't. I went through thirty tickets till I found one ending in 1508, my birthday.
Ammavan said the top one had the same chance. But it can't, right? I chose this one. I looked properly. The top one is just random.
The draw is on Friday. I've already planned what to say when it wins. I keep checking the ticket on the fridge, as if looking after it helps.
If it loses, I'll just pick even more carefully next time.
Write back and tell me I'm right.
Nitin

qa.q: What did the ticket Nitin chose end in?
qa.a: The ticket Nitin chose ended in 1508, Nitin's birthday.

qa.q: Why does the chosen ticket feel luckier to Nitin?
qa.a: Nitin feels hopeful and in control, as if looking through thirty tickets carefully must count for more than taking the top one.

qa.q: What could Yamini write back to help Nitin see the odds clearly?
qa.a: Yamini could explain that every ticket in the rack has the same chance, just as Ammavan said, so choosing harder cannot change a draw.

qa.q: How might Ammavan see Nitin's careful choosing?
qa.a: Ammavan seems to find it harmless fun but says plainly that the top ticket had the same chance.

grounding: Shows a teenager who believes choosing a lottery ticket with a personal number gives better odds than a random one.

passage: Gopika, you'll think I'm silly, but here's what happened at the Christmas fair last week. They had a raffle for a new bicycle, tickets numbered one to five hundred, ten rupees each. You could take a ticket from the pile, or pay five rupees more and choose your own number. Obviously I chose. Seventeen: my birthday and my jersey number. I even rubbed it for luck. Everyone who took a random one, I felt sorry for them; they'd left it to chance, and I had picked. The draw was at six. Number three hundred and something won. A little kid who had grabbed the top ticket off the pile. I stood there thinking, but I chose mine. Anyway, that's how Tenzin spent fifteen rupees and learned the bicycle doesn't care about birthdays.

qa.a: Seventeen, Tenzin's birthday and jersey number.

qa.q: Why did Tenzin feel sorry for the people who took random tickets?
qa.a: Choosing the number felt like taking control, so Tenzin felt confident and a bit superior, as if picking improved the odds.

qa.q: What could Tenzin ask before paying extra next time?
qa.a: Tenzin could ask whether choosing changes how the winning ticket is drawn, and remember that every number had the same chance.

qa.q: How might the little kid see the raffle?
qa.a: The little kid just grabbed the top ticket and won, probably thrilled and without any idea that choosing was supposed to matter.

grounding: Shows a teenager paying extra to choose a raffle number, believing choice improves the odds of pure chance.
